Market order.long:
A market order instructs the exchange to trade immediately at the best price currently available. It does not name a price; it names a quantity and a direction, and the matching engine fills it against whatever is resting on the other side of the book, taking the best-priced orders first and walking deeper if the size demands it.

What it buys you is certainty of execution. What it costs you is the spread at minimum, and worse in thin conditions. On MNQ with a one-tick spread, a single-contract market order gives up around $0.50 to cross; in a fast market or at size, the fill can land several points away from the quote you saw, at $2 per point.

It is the right tool when getting out, or in, matters more than the price of doing so — most obviously when exiting a position that has hit its invalidation.

Where people get fooled: treating the on-screen quote as the price they will get. The quote is the best price for the first units only. Slippage on entry is an annoyance; slippage on a panicked exit in a thin market is where the real cost lives.
Market order.usage: Typically reserved for moments where execution certainty outranks price — exits at invalidation, or liquid instruments where the spread is a known, small cost.

Limit order.long:
A limit order rests in the book at a stated price and will only fill at that price or better. A buy limit at 21,400 on MNQ can fill at 21,400 or lower, never higher. Until it fills, it sits in the queue behind every order placed at that price before it.

Mechanically you are providing liquidity rather than taking it: someone else must cross the spread into your order. That earns you the spread instead of paying it, and on some venues a rebate, but it costs you certainty — price can approach your level, touch it, and leave without filling you.

Queue position matters more than most retail traders realise. At a heavily bid level, price can trade at your price repeatedly while orders ahead of you absorb every fill. Getting filled easily often means the level broke and everyone in the queue got filled — the fills you receive most readily are the ones you may want least.

Where people get fooled: reading a touch of the level as a fill. A limit needs price to trade through it, or enough volume at it to reach your place in the queue. The trade that ran without you was never yours.
Limit order.usage: Standard for entries where price matters more than participation, and for exits at pre-chosen targets; the unfilled limit that would have worked is part of the deal, not a malfunction.

Stop order.long:
A stop order is a resting instruction that stays inactive until price touches a trigger level, at which point it becomes a market order and executes at whatever price is then available. A sell stop sits below the current price; a buy stop sits above it. Nothing about the order guarantees the trigger price itself.

Its two jobs are opposite in character: as protection, it closes a position when the trade's premise has failed; as an entry, it joins a move only once price proves it can reach a level. In both cases the mechanism is identical — touch, convert, execute at market.

Because the conversion is to a market order, the fill inherits every property of one. On MNQ at $2 per point, a stop triggered in an orderly market might slip a tick or two; the same stop triggered through a data release can fill five or ten points through the level.

Where people get fooled: expecting the stop price to be the fill price. The trigger is a level; the fill is wherever liquidity is when the market order arrives. Gaps and halts make this vivid — the stop executes where trading resumes, not where the trigger sat.
Stop order.usage: Used both as the standing protective exit and as a breakout-style entry; in either role the working assumption is trigger certainty, not price certainty.

Stop-limit.long:
A stop-limit order rests like a stop, but on trigger it becomes a limit order rather than a market order. You set two prices: the stop price that activates it, and the limit price that caps what you will accept. A sell stop-limit at 21,400 with a limit of 21,395 will, once 21,400 trades, work as a sell limit at 21,395 — it fills at 21,395 or better, or not at all.

The appeal is control: no fill more than your stated distance through the trigger. The cost is the one property a protective order exists to provide — certainty of exit. If price gaps or sweeps through both the stop and the limit, the order sits unfilled while the position keeps losing.

On MNQ at $2 per point, a five-point limit offset caps slippage at $10 per contract. In an orderly tape that cap is rarely tested. The fast tape is the only tape where slippage gets large — and it is exactly when the limit is most likely to be left behind.

Where people get fooled: using a stop-limit as their protective stop to avoid slippage, then discovering in a flush that they avoided the fill instead. The saved ticks are visible on every ordinary day; the unprotected disaster is rare, and total.
Stop-limit.usage: Sometimes chosen for entries where chasing past a level is unacceptable; as protection, its non-fill risk is the entire trade-off.

Take profit.long:
A take profit is a resting limit order at the level where you intend to bank the trade — a sell limit above the market for a long, a buy limit below it for a short. Mechanically it is nothing more exotic than a limit order with a job title: it fills at your price or better, or it does not fill.

Because it is a limit, it inherits limit-order behaviour at the level. Price can touch the target and reverse without filling you if orders ahead in the queue soak up the volume. Fills that come easily are usually the ones where price traded straight through — which is fine, since through is what you wanted.

Placing it at order entry rather than deciding later changes the trade's character. A target chosen in advance is a measurement of the idea; one improvised mid-trade is usually a measurement of your mood at the time.

Where people get fooled: setting the target at a round number or an obvious prior high where everyone else's target also sits. The queue there is longest and the reversal risk highest. A target a tick or two in front of the obvious level trades a sliver of profit for better odds of actually being filled.
Take profit.usage: Paired with a stop as a bracket so the trade can resolve without attendance; the target's location comes from structure, not from the profit figure it implies.

Trailing stop.long:
A trailing stop is a stop order whose trigger follows price at a fixed distance as the trade moves in your favour, and holds still when it moves against you. A ten-point trail on a long MNQ position ratchets the trigger up each time price makes a new high, always ten points behind the best price reached; it never widens. On trigger it converts to a market order like any other stop.

Where the trail is maintained matters. Some platforms hold the logic server-side or at the exchange; others run it in your local software, where a dropped connection freezes the trail at its last level while the position keeps moving.

The distance is the entire design decision. Trail inside the market's normal noise and you will be taken out by fluctuation that means nothing; trail outside it and you hand back a large fixed slice of every winner. A trail calibrated to recent volatility at least fails honestly.

Where people get fooled: believing a trail locks in the on-screen profit. It locks in a trigger, and the fill is a market-order fill — in a fast reversal the exit lands beyond the trail distance. The other trap is tightening the trail out of nerves, which converts a trend-following exit into a noise-following one.
Trailing stop.usage: Common for letting a winner run without manual management; the trailing distance is usually anchored to volatility or structure rather than to a comfortable-sounding number.

OCO.long:
OCO stands for one-cancels-other: two orders linked so that a fill on either automatically cancels the other. The standard use is a stop and a take profit protecting the same position — whichever level trades first closes the trade, and the surviving order is pulled instead of lingering as a live instruction to open a fresh position.

Without the link, the leftover order is a genuine hazard. A target that fills while a forgotten stop still rests below the market is no longer protection; it is a new short waiting to trigger. The OCO removes that failure mode mechanically rather than relying on you to remember.

The implementation detail worth knowing is where the link lives. Some venues support OCO natively at the exchange; many brokers simulate it on their servers or in your platform. A simulated link depends on that server or platform being up and connected at the moment one leg fills.

Where people get fooled: partial fills. If half the position exits at the target, the linked stop must be reduced to match the remainder — some platforms do this automatically, others cancel the sibling entirely or leave it at full quantity. Discovering which kind you have during a live trade is the expensive way to learn it.
OCO.usage: The default wrapper for a stop-and-target pair; worth testing on a simulator to see exactly how the platform handles partial fills before trusting it with size.

Bracket order.long:
A bracket order is an entry order with a stop loss and a take profit attached, the two exits linked as an OCO pair that goes live the moment the entry fills. One instruction defines the whole trade: where you get in, where you are wrong, where you are done. Buy MNQ at 21,400 with a bracket of 15 points either way and the platform works a sell stop at 21,385 and a sell limit at 21,415 from the instant of the fill.

The mechanical value is the elimination of the gap between being filled and being protected. A trader placing exits by hand after entry is unprotected for seconds at best — and for as long as the platform, the connection, or their own attention fails at worst.

It also forces the exit decision to happen before the position exists, while you are still capable of making it dispassionately. Fifteen points either side is easy to type before entry and strangely difficult to honour after it.

Where people get fooled: assuming the bracket lives at the exchange. On many platforms the child orders are held broker-side or locally and submitted on fill; an outage in between can leave the position naked. Knowing where your bracket actually resides is not optional knowledge.
Bracket order.usage: Standard practice for defining the full trade before entry, particularly on instruments and sessions where manual reaction time is not to be trusted.

GTC / day order.long:
These are the two most common time-in-force settings — the instruction that tells the exchange how long an order should remain working. A day order dies automatically at the end of the trading session if unfilled. A GTC order, good-till-cancelled, keeps resting session after session until it fills, is cancelled, or hits the broker's maximum age, often somewhere between 30 and 90 days.

The mechanics are trivial; the consequences are not. A day-order stop protecting a position held overnight expires at the close, leaving the position unprotected at the next open — precisely when gaps happen. A GTC limit placed weeks ago fills the moment price finally reaches it, whether or not the idea behind it still exists.

Neither default is safe; they fail in opposite directions. Day orders fail by quietly disappearing while the exposure remains. GTC orders fail by quietly persisting after the reason for them is gone.

Where people get fooled: the stale GTC fill. Price crashes into a months-old buy limit and delivers a position whose thesis expired long ago, at a moment chosen entirely by the market. The order did exactly what it was told; the instruction had simply outlived its author's memory of giving it.
GTC / day order.usage: The time-in-force setting is checked rather than assumed — especially on protective stops for positions held past the session, and in any regular review of resting orders.

IOC / FOK.long:
Immediate-or-cancel and fill-or-kill are time-in-force settings for orders that refuse to rest. An IOC order executes whatever portion of it can fill immediately against the book and cancels the remainder. A FOK order is stricter: it must fill in its entirety immediately, or the whole order is cancelled. Neither ever sits in the queue.

The difference is what you tolerate. Send an IOC buy for 10 contracts with 6 available at your price and you get 6, with the other 4 cancelled. Send the same as FOK and you get nothing at all. IOC accepts partial outcomes; FOK treats the order as indivisible.

These exist mostly for execution problems where resting is itself a cost — signalling intent to the market, or legging into spreads where a partial fill leaves an unbalanced position. FOK is the natural fit for the spread leg; IOC for taking what liquidity is present without advertising the rest.

Where people get fooled: assuming immediate means the full size at my price. An IOC limit fills only what is available within the limit; the cancelled remainder is easy to miss on a busy screen, leaving you sized smaller than you believe while your stop and target still assume the full quantity.
IOC / FOK.usage: Niche settings for most retail workflows, but the mechanics matter when a partial position would be worse than none — multi-leg trades being the obvious case.

No stop loss.long:
Trading without a stop means carrying a position whose worst case is undefined. Nothing at the exchange limits the loss; the exit will happen only when you act, when the broker liquidates you at a margin call, or when the account is gone. That is the whole mechanism: there is not one.

The honest argument for it exists and is narrow. A resting stop can be filled by a brief sweep that immediately reverses, and some traders on some instruments judge that cost worse than managing risk another way — through option structures with defined risk, through sizes so small the worst plausible move is survivable, or through hard exits executed by rule. Every version of that argument replaces the stop with something; none replaces it with nothing.

Without a resting order, the exit depends on your presence, your data feed, your platform and your nerve, all functioning at the worst moment of the trade. Gaps, halts and overnight moves do not wait for attendance.

Where people get fooled: surviving it. Positions without stops usually come back, because most adverse moves do — and each recovery trains the habit until the one unbounded move ends it. The account is then not damaged but finished, and the lesson arrives with nothing left to apply it to.
No stop loss.usage: Where traders forgo resting stops, the defensible variants substitute defined-risk structures or drastic size reduction; the version with no substitute at all is an account-lifetime bet, not a technique.

Market-on-close.long:
A market-on-close order executes in the closing auction at the official closing price. Rather than trading against the continuous book, MOC orders are collected by the exchange, netted against each other and against limit-on-close interest, and filled together in the single print that becomes the day's close.

Exchanges enforce a cutoff — on US equities, MOC orders generally cannot be entered or amended in the final minutes before the bell, so the auction's imbalance can be published and offset. Miss the cutoff and the order is rejected; there is no late entry into the auction.

The attraction is the price itself. The close is the most liquid single moment of the day on many instruments, the benchmark that funds are measured against, and the price at which end-of-day systems assume trades happen. An MOC is how an assumption about closing fills gets honoured in practice.

Where people get fooled: assuming the auction price will resemble the last price they watched. Large imbalances can push the close well away from the final minutes of the continuous tape, and an MOC takes whatever the auction prints — that is its definition. The certainty on offer is participation at the close, not the level the close turns out to be.
Market-on-close.usage: The natural instrument where closing-price execution is the point; the cutoff rules of the specific exchange matter more than the order type's simplicity suggests.

Limit-on-close.long:
A limit-on-close order participates in the closing auction, but only if the auction price satisfies its limit. A buy LOC at 50.00 fills at the official close if that close is 50.00 or lower; if the auction prints higher, the order expires unfilled. It is the closing-auction counterpart of an ordinary limit order, subject to the same entry cutoffs as market-on-close orders.

The mechanism gives you a bounded version of the close. An MOC accepts whatever the auction prints; an LOC states the worst price you will take and lets the fill go if the auction lands beyond it. In exchange, you reintroduce the possibility of missing the trade entirely.

That trade-off tracks the ordinary market-versus-limit decision, compressed into a single moment. When participating at the close is the point — a rebalance, a benchmark-tracking exit — the LOC's non-fill is a real cost. When price discipline is the point, the MOC's blank cheque is the real cost.

Where people get fooled: treating the pre-close indicative price as a promise. The published imbalance and indicative match price move as late interest arrives, and a limit set snugly against the indicative can be left behind by the final print. The auction owes you nothing but its rules.
Limit-on-close.usage: Used where closing-price execution is wanted only within a stated bound; the unfilled case needs a plan, since the session ends with it.

Midpoint / pegged order.long:
A pegged order rests at a price defined relative to the quote rather than as a fixed number, and re-prices automatically as the quote moves. The most common form is the midpoint peg, which floats at the midpoint between the best bid and ask. Buy pegged to the mid on a market quoted 100.00 at 100.02 and your order works at 100.01, moving with every update of the quote.

The attraction is the spread: a midpoint fill splits it, so both sides do better than crossing. These orders are typically undisplayed and are the standard mechanism inside dark pools, where matching at the midpoint of the public quote is the whole business model.

What you give up is priority and certainty. An undisplayed midpoint order fills only when a counterparty arrives willing to trade there, and displayed quotes at the same effective price are generally served first. It is a patient tool, not an urgent one.

Where people get fooled: forgetting that the peg follows the quote wherever it goes. If the market runs away, the pegged order runs with it, faithfully offering the midpoint of prices that keep getting worse — it never chases in the sense of crossing the spread, but it never holds a level either. A peg is a formula, not an opinion.
Midpoint / pegged order.usage: Mostly a cost-reduction tool for patient orders in liquid names; the fill-rate penalty of resting undisplayed is the price of the saved spread.

Hidden / reserve order.long:
Both are ways to rest size without displaying it. A hidden order shows nothing at all: it sits in the book, executable but invisible in the displayed quote. A reserve order — the iceberg — displays a small slice and holds the rest back; each time the visible portion fills, the exchange replenishes it from the reserve until the full size is done.

The purpose is to avoid moving the market with your own intention. A 500-lot displayed on the bid is information every participant can trade against; the same size shown 10 lots at a time is much quieter. Exchanges charge for this quietness in priority: hidden volume typically ranks behind displayed volume at the same price, and each iceberg refresh joins the queue anew.

The result is a fill-rate cost. Displayed orders at your price get served first, and in a fast move the hidden portion can be left behind entirely.

Where people get fooled: believing invisibility means undetectability. A price level that keeps refilling after every execution is a pattern, and participants watch for exactly that — repeated prints at one price behind a small persistent quote is an iceberg announcing itself. Hiding size reduces its footprint; it does not remove it.
Hidden / reserve order.usage: Relevant mostly at institutional size or in thin books; for small retail orders the display decision changes little beyond queue priority.

Time in force.long:
Time in force is the field on an order that says how long it remains alive. Day orders expire at session end. GTC rests until cancelled or aged out by the broker. IOC executes what it can instantly and cancels the rest. FOK fills completely and instantly or not at all. Good-till-date variants expire when you say; on-open and on-close variants exist only inside the auctions. The matching engine treats the setting as law.

It is the least glamorous field on the ticket and the source of a disproportionate share of order-management accidents, because platforms fill it in silently with a default. Some default to day, some to GTC, and some default differently for stops than for limits.

The field also interacts with sessions in ways worth checking: whether a day order on a futures platform dies at the equity close, the electronic session end, or the daily maintenance break varies by broker and instrument.

Where people get fooled: never choosing at all. The trader who does not know their platform's default discovers it operationally — a protective stop that vanished at the close, or a limit from three weeks ago that filled into a news event. The order did what the field said; nobody had read the field.
Time in force.usage: Worth a one-time audit per platform: what the defaults are, per order type, and when the session boundaries that expire day orders actually occur.

Stop-market vs stop-limit trade-off.long:
A triggered stop-market becomes a market order: it will fill, at whatever price the book offers. A triggered stop-limit becomes a limit order: it will fill at your stated price or better, or it will not fill. Every choice between them is a choice between guaranteed exit with unknown cost and capped cost with unknown exit.

The deciding question is what the order is for. A protective stop exists for the scenario where the trade is failing, and the worst versions of that scenario — the flush, the news spike, the gap — are exactly the conditions in which a stop-limit's cap is most likely to leave the order stranded. Protection that can fail to protect in the bad tail has its priorities inverted.

For entries the logic softens. A stop-limit entry that misses its fill costs an opportunity, not an open-ended loss; capping how far you will chase a breakout is a defensible design.

Where people get fooled: pricing the trade-off from the ordinary days. On most triggers the two order types fill within a tick or two of each other, and the stop-limit's saved slippage looks free. The comparison that matters happens on the day the market goes disorderly — the day the stop-market pays a few points and the stop-limit pays the whole move.
Stop-market vs stop-limit trade-off.usage: A common convention is stop-market for protection and stop-limit only for entries; whichever way it goes, the choice is made per purpose, not per mood.

Bracket on entry.long:
Bracket on entry means the stop and target are attached to the entry order itself, so the moment the entry fills, both exits are already working as a linked OCO pair. The alternative — filling first and placing exits afterwards — leaves a window in which the position exists and its protection does not.

That window is short on a good day and unbounded on a bad one. A platform freeze, a connection drop, a phone call, a moment of hesitation while price moves: the manual-exit workflow depends on nothing going wrong in the seconds after the fill, which is an odd foundation for a risk-control system.

There is a second, quieter benefit. Deciding the stop and target before the entry order goes in means deciding them while flat, when the levels are a judgement about the market rather than a negotiation with an open profit or loss. The bracket makes the pre-commitment mechanical.

Where people get fooled: setting a template bracket — the same fixed points on every trade — and letting it override the structure the trade was based on. Fifteen points is not a stop level; it is a distance. If the level where the idea fails sits twenty points away, a fifteen-point template stop is a random exit wearing a seatbelt.
Bracket on entry.usage: Most platforms can attach default brackets to entries; the defaults handle the protection gap, and the levels still get adjusted to the actual trade's structure.

Partial fill.long:
A partial fill is an order executed for less than its full quantity. A resting limit for 10 contracts may fill 4 and leave 6 working; the counterparty flow at that price simply ran out. Nothing has gone wrong — the order stays in the book, at its queue position, for the remainder. Marketable orders can also partially fill when displayed liquidity is thinner than the order, with the remainder either resting or cancelling according to the time-in-force setting.

The bookkeeping consequences are the real content. A position of 4 contracts protected by a stop for 10 is not protected; it is a position plus a pending order to reverse. Exits inherit the same problem in the other direction: scaling out with limits can leave odd remainders that no longer match the plan's arithmetic.

Some platforms adjust linked orders automatically when a parent order partially fills; others do not, and the difference is discoverable only by reading the documentation or by being burned.

Where people get fooled: planning and journaling as if fills were binary. The trader who thinks in units of all-or-nothing meets a market that deals in whatever was available. Odd remainders, mismatched brackets and leftover orders working overnight all come from the same blind spot.
Partial fill.usage: Behaviour to verify per platform: what happens to attached stops and targets when an entry half-fills, and what the remainder does at session end.

Order rejection.long:
A rejection is an order refused before it ever reaches the book — by the broker's risk checks or by the exchange itself. Common causes: insufficient margin, a price outside the day's permitted bands, an increment the instrument does not trade in, a closed session, a size above limits, or a product the account is not permissioned for. The order does not rest, does not queue, does not exist.

Mechanically a rejection is immediate and comes with a reason, but platforms vary widely in how loudly they surface it. A rejected entry costs an opportunity; a rejected protective stop costs the protection while the position runs unguarded, and that asymmetry is the entire reason rejections deserve attention.

Rejections also cluster at the worst times, because the conditions that cause them — volatility bands hit, margin stretched, sessions transitioning — are the conditions of stressed markets. The order most likely to bounce is the one sent in a hurry.

Where people get fooled: treating the act of sending as the ancestor of a fill. Sent is not working, and working is not filled. The trader who fires an order and looks away has collapsed three states into one hope. Confirming that the stop is actually working, especially after a reconnect, costs seconds.
Order rejection.usage: The working, filled or rejected status of every order gets confirmed visually, and protective orders get re-verified after any disconnection or platform restart.

Long.long:
To be long is to own the exposure: you profit if price rises and lose if it falls. In shares this is literal ownership of the asset, settled into your account, with the worst case being a fall to zero — severe, but arithmetically bounded. In futures, long means holding a bought contract against margin; you own an obligation rather than a thing, and the position is marked to market daily with gains and losses settled in cash.

The asymmetry with short is structural. A long position's loss is capped at the amount invested while its gain is uncapped; there is no borrow to pay, nothing to be recalled, no forced buy-in. Equity markets have also drifted upward over long horizons, which makes long the side with the structural tailwind — and exactly why it deserves suspicion in the short term, because everyone finds buying easier.

Leverage rewrites the arithmetic. A leveraged long can lose more than its margin, and the bounded-at-zero comfort applies to the asset, not to a geared position in it.

Where people get fooled: mistaking the comfort of the long side for an edge. Long feels like optimism and ownership, and platforms, media and instinct all make it the path of least resistance — none of which says anything about whether this long, here, now, has any merit.
Long.usage: The default side for most participants, which is worth remembering whenever everyone agrees; a long thesis still needs an invalidation level like any other.

Short.long:
To be short is to profit from a fall in price, and how you get there depends on the instrument. In equities you borrow shares, sell them, and later buy them back to return; the borrow costs a fee that ranges from negligible to punitive, the shares can be recalled, and a forced buy-in can close the position at the lender's convenience rather than yours. In futures there is no borrow at all: you simply sell a contract first, and the mechanics are the exact mirror of a long.

The defining risk of equity shorting is that losses are uncapped. A share bought at 20 can only lose 20; a share shorted at 20 can rise to 60, or 200. An adverse move also grows the position's weight in the account as it grows, the reverse of a losing long shrinking.

Add the running costs — borrow fees, dividends owed while short, margin interest — and time itself works against the position in a way it does not for a long.

Where people get fooled: shorting something because it is obviously ridiculous. Overvaluation is not a catalyst, and crowded shorts are the raw fuel of squeezes — the more untenable the price, the more violent the rally that forced buyers create. Being right eventually is not the same trade as staying solvent until eventually arrives.
Short.usage: Futures and CFDs make the mechanics symmetrical; equity shorting adds borrow logistics and uncapped tail risk that sizing has to respect from the outset.

Position size.long:
Position size is the quantity you actually hold — contracts, shares, lots. It is the one variable under full control at entry, and it converts a market distance into a money amount. The arithmetic runs backwards from risk: decide the account risk for the trade, measure the stop distance the setup requires, and the size falls out. Risking $100 on an MNQ trade with a 25-point stop at $2 per point means $50 of risk per contract: two contracts, no discretion required.

Run the arithmetic in that order and every trade carries the same weight regardless of how wide its stop is. Run it in the other order — pick a size you like, then find a stop that keeps the loss acceptable — and the stop migrates to where the money wants it rather than where the idea fails.

Size is also where conviction quietly leaks in. The same setup taken at triple size because it feels certain is a different bet with the same name.

Where people get fooled: adjusting size by feel after wins and losses. Doubling after a loss to get it back is martingale by instalments; swelling after a streak is how the best month funds the worst one. Size decided by formula is dull, which is the point.
Position size.usage: Computed from stop distance and a fixed per-trade risk before entry; the formula's dullness is a feature that survives both streaks and slumps.

Entry / exit.long:
Entry and exit are the two transactions that bracket every trade: the fill that opens the exposure and the fill that ends it. Everything a trade will ever be — its risk, its profit, its duration, its quality as a decision — is fixed by these two prices and the size carried between them.

The attention they receive is lopsided. Entries are where the searching, the indicators and the content industry live, because entries are optional and infinitely postponable — you can always wait for a better one. Exits are compulsory. Every position must end, either by plan or by improvisation, and improvised exits made under an open profit or loss are where accounts actually bleed.

A workable habit is to define the exit pair before the entry exists: the price where the idea is wrong and the price where it has delivered. An entry without both is not early; it is incomplete.

Where people get fooled: grading the pair separately. A good entry closed in panic is a bad trade; a mediocre entry managed by rule is often a fine one. The result lives in the relationship between the two fills, and polishing the entry while improvising the exit optimises the half that matters less.
Entry / exit.usage: Both prices, plus size, get written down before the order goes in; the exit half of the plan is the half that gets tested under stress.

Flat.long:
Flat means holding no position: no exposure, no open risk, nothing marked to market against you. It is the state between trades, and it is the only state in which the market cannot charge you for anything.

It is worth treating flat as a position in its own right — the one you hold whenever no available trade clears your bar. Every moment flat is a decision not to hold everything you could have held, which is why it can feel like falling behind while others are in. That feeling is the cost of the position; the benefit is that your capital and your judgement are fully available for the next real opportunity, uncontaminated by an open profit or loss shading every read of the chart.

Going flat also has a mechanical role in a trading day: after a loss that broke the plan, after hitting a daily limit, before news you have no business holding through. Flat is the reset that always works.

Where people get fooled: being unable to stay there. The compulsion to always have a position on treats flat as a malfunction to be fixed at the next plausible excuse — which converts a set of chosen trades into a permanent rolling exposure chosen by boredom. The trader who cannot be flat has delegated sizing to restlessness.
Flat.usage: Flat is the default state, departed from for specific reasons; daily loss limits and news blackouts are typically enforced by returning to it.

Scaling in.long:
Scaling in is building a position in planned instalments rather than all at once — a third at the initial signal, a third on confirmation, a third on the retest, each tranche and its trigger decided before the first order goes in. The total intended size and the stop for the whole position exist from the start; only the entry is spread out.

The mechanics cut both ways. Adding as the trade works means the average price is worse than the first fill, so the best trades earn less per unit than a full-size entry would have. In exchange, the trades that fail immediately fail at partial size. You are trading maximum profit on the winners for a smaller bill on the fast losers.

The plan is what separates scaling in from its disreputable cousin. Instalments added at predetermined levels within a fixed total size is scaling in; size added because the position is losing and the average could be improved is averaging down wearing better clothes.

Where people get fooled: letting the tranches grow. If each add follows the pre-set schedule, fine; if the third tranche gets doubled because conviction has swollen with the open profit, the final size was set by mood near the top of the move — and the point of maximum size becomes the point of maximum vulnerability.
Scaling in.usage: Tranches, triggers and total size are fixed in advance; the whole structure still answers to one stop and one invalidation.

Scaling out.long:
Scaling out is exiting a position in parts — say half at a first target, a quarter at a second, the rest run with a trailing stop. Each exit is an ordinary order; the technique is the schedule.

The arithmetic deserves honest inspection, because it is unflattering. Losers hit the stop at full size, while winners are progressively trimmed, so the winners are paid at reduced size exactly when they perform. A strategy scaled out of will usually show a smoother equity curve and a lower total result than the same strategy exited whole at the final target — you are buying comfort with expectancy.

Comfort has real value, though. Banking a first tranche makes the remainder easier to hold to a distant target, and for some traders the scaled version is the only version they can actually execute. A plan that survives contact with your own nerves beats a better plan that does not.

Where people get fooled: crediting the smoothness to skill. The journal shows mostly green days because something almost always gets banked at the first target — while the account grinds sideways, because the full-size losses quietly outweigh the trimmed wins. If scaling out is used, the whole-position result per trade is the number to audit, not the comforting count of partial wins.
Scaling out.usage: If used, the exit schedule is fixed in advance and the trade is judged on its blended result per position, not on how many tranches finished green.

Runner.long:
A runner is the final portion of a scaled-out position, left working after earlier tranches have been banked, in the hope of catching the occasional extended move. Mechanically it is just a smaller position with a stop — usually moved to breakeven or trailed — and either a distant target or none at all.

The honest case for runners is that trend-shaped profits are rare and large, and a small permanent claim on them can pay for many ordinary trades. The honest case against is arithmetic: the runner is the smallest slice of the position, riding the moves that would have paid the most, and many runners get stopped at or near breakeven, contributing little beyond the feeling of prudence.

Which case wins is an empirical question about your own trades, answerable only from a journal that records what runners actually earned against what exiting fully at the final target would have.

Where people get fooled: the runner as lottery ticket. Because it feels free after the earlier exits — house money, in the usual phrase — its management goes slack: stops trailed by vibe, targets abandoned, the position held through reversals a full-size trade would never be allowed to sit through. A runner is still capital at risk, and house money is still money.
Runner.usage: Runner rules — size, stop treatment, abandonment conditions — get written like any other exit rule, and their contribution gets measured against the simpler alternative.

Averaging down.long:
Averaging down is adding to a losing position so the average entry price improves. Buy at 100, buy again at 90, and the position breaks even at 95 instead of 100 — the arithmetic is real, and it is the whole of the appeal. Every add lowers the price the market must return to before the mistake is forgiven.

What the arithmetic hides is what is being purchased: more size, precisely as the market disagrees harder. The trade's premise is being disproved and the response is to enlarge exposure to it. Risk that was defined at entry becomes undefined, because a habit of adding into decline has no natural stop — any level that would have ended the trade becomes a level to buy more.

The practice survives because it usually works. Most dips revert, most averaged positions escape at the improved breakeven, and each escape reinforces the method. But the distribution has a tail: the position that keeps falling, absorbing add after add, until it is the account.

Where people get fooled: confusing it with planned scaling. Instalment entries with a fixed total size and a stop for the whole structure are a plan. Adds improvised in drawdown, sized by the desire to break even, are the behaviour that ends accounts — and the method's failures are not around afterwards to post about it.
Averaging down.usage: The diagnostic question is asked before entry: is a lower add pre-planned with fixed total size and a hard stop, or would it be invented in the drawdown?

Breakeven stop.long:
A breakeven stop is a protective stop moved to the entry price once the trade has travelled some distance in your favour. From that point the worst case is, in theory, a scratch: the open risk on the trade drops to roughly zero while the upside keeps working.

Two mechanical caveats live inside roughly. The fill on a triggered stop is a market-order fill, so a fast reversal exits slightly through entry, and costs — commissions and the spread — mean a true scratch actually books a small loss. Breakeven is a region, not a point.

The design question is when to move it. Entry prices are personal, not structural: the market does not know or care where you got in, so a stop at your entry sits at a level with no market meaning. Move it too early and the ordinary pullback that would have preceded the winning leg stops you out flat; the idea was right and paid nothing.

Where people get fooled: counting the scratches as free. A rule that converts winners into breakevens has a cost that never appears as a red number — the journal fills with harmless-looking scratches that were, counterfactually, the winning trades. If a breakeven rule is used, the honest audit is what those scratched trades went on to do.
Breakeven stop.usage: Commonly triggered by structure — a new swing forming beyond entry — rather than by profit alone, so the stop's new home means something to the market and not just to the account.
